sections.title: Lesson 1.1: New Issues and the Primary Market
sections.overview: The primary market is where issuers (corporations, municipalities, federal government/agencies) sell securities directly to investors to raise capital, receiving the proceeds themselves. The Securities Act of 1933 ('Paper Act') governs new issues by requiring full and fair disclosure via SEC registration and prospectus delivery — unless an exemption applies. This lesson covers issuer types, underwriting commitments, the IPO process (registration, cooling-off, effective date), shelf offerings, prospectus delivery rules, and exempt issuers/issues/transactions.
key_concepts: Primary market = issuer transactions; issuer receives proceeds. Secondary market = investor-to-investor; issuer is NOT involved (exception: corporate buybacks/tender offers).
IPO = first public offering of an issuer; APO (follow-on / subsequent / additional primary offering) = subsequent primary offerings by an already-public issuer.
Combination/split/hybrid offering = mix of newly issued shares (proceeds to issuer) and existing shareholder shares (proceeds to selling holders).
Issuers: corporations (stocks/bonds), municipalities (munis), U.S. Treasury (govies), federal agencies.
NMS securities = listed on a national exchange or Nasdaq; non-NMS = not so listed.

Underwriters = broker-dealers/investment bankers that bring issues to market, often as a syndicate (joint venture sharing risk/profit) with a managing underwriter; selling group members assist without capital commitment or inventory risk.

Firm commitment underwriting: underwriters act as PRINCIPAL — they buy the entire issue from the issuer and resell at POP, earning the spread; underwriters bear the risk of unsold shares. Firms may NEVER guarantee repurchase at POP.

Best efforts underwriting: underwriters act as AGENT — no commitment to buy; issuer bears the risk. Subtypes: All-or-None (AON: sell all or cancel; funds held in escrow) and Mini-Max (must hit minimum floor before any sale; can expand up to maximum ceiling).

Investor classes: Retail (own assets, less sophisticated, higher disclosure standards); Institutional (banks, insurance cos., pensions, hedge funds, mutual funds, investment advisers); QIBs (institutions owning/investing ≥$100M on discretionary basis); Accredited (used only in primary market).

Accredited investor (Rule 501, Reg D): all institutionals; insiders (officers, directors, 10%+ owners); income ≥$200K individually (or $300K joint) for last 2 years with same expected this year; net worth ≥$1M excluding primary residence; certain professional licenses (Series 7, 65, 82) in good standing.
Municipal advisors: advise municipalities on debt issuance; CANNOT switch to underwriter role on the same issue and cannot be compensated as underwriter.

Registration statement (S-1) discloses: business description, officers/directors (names, addresses, salaries, 5-year history), insider ownership and 10%+ owners, capitalization, use of proceeds, legal proceedings. Issuer (not underwriter) is responsible for accuracy.
Cooling-off period: minimum 20 calendar days from filing; SEC may issue a deficiency letter (clock pauses and resumes where left off, does NOT restart).

During cooling-off: NO sales/solicitations; permitted activities = tombstone ads, preliminary prospectus (red herring), gathering indications of interest (nonbinding), due diligence meetings, blue-sky (state) registration.

Tombstone ad: only advertisement permitted during cooling-off; optional; not filed with SEC; limited content (issuer name, security type, # shares, POP or range, syndicate members) plus required disclaimer that offer is made only by prospectus.
Red herring (preliminary prospectus): used to gather indications of interest; no final POP required; must be provided to any interested customer during cooling-off.
Final prospectus: delivered on/after effective date; adds POP and effective date; must precede or accompany all sales confirmations; contains SEC disclaimer.
SEC does NOT approve, endorse, or pass on the merits of any new issue — language is that SEC 'allows' or 'releases.'

Shelf registration: lets a seasoned public issuer register now, sell later — good for 2 years (3 years for a WKSI; any major-exchange-listed issuer typically qualifies). A supplemental prospectus must be filed before each takedown.
Post-effective prospectus delivery in secondary market: IPO NMS = 25 days; APO NMS = 0 days; IPO non-NMS = 90 days; APO non-NMS = 40 days. SEC-website access satisfies delivery.

Exempt issuers (issuer-based exemption): U.S. government; municipalities; national & state banks (NOT bank holding companies); S&Ls/building & loans; charitable, religious, educational, nonprofit; common carriers (e.g., railroad equipment trust certificates).

Exempt issues (security-based): commercial paper, bankers' acceptances, and other short-term debt with maturity ≤270 days; fixed insurance policies and fixed annuities (NOT variable products — variable annuities, VLI, VUL must be registered).
Reg A (Tier 1): up to $20M in 12 months (max $6M from selling shareholders); coordinated SEC + state review; no investment limit.

Reg A (Tier 2): up to $75M in 12 months (max $22.5M from selling shareholders); SEC review only (preempts state); audited financials; ongoing reports. Non-accredited Tier 2 investors limited to greater of 10% of net worth or 10% of annual net income (self-certification).
Reg A excludes investment companies (private equity, VC, hedge funds). Both tiers permit general solicitation/advertising.

Rule 147 (intrastate): exempt if issuer's principal office is in-state AND all purchasers are state residents; issuer must meet one 80% test (80% income, 80% assets, or 80% proceeds in-state) OR majority of employees in-state; any underwriting BD must be in-state; resales restricted to in-state residents for 6 months.

Reg D Rule 506(b) (private placement): unlimited capital; unlimited accredited investors; up to 35 non-accredited (must be sophisticated and receive disclosure equivalent to a prospectus); no general solicitation; Form D filed with SEC.
Reg D Rule 506(c): permits general solicitation/advertising BUT ALL purchasers must be accredited AND issuer must take reasonable steps to verify accredited status.

Private placement stock = restricted / unregistered / letter stock / legend stock — investor signs an investment letter; certificate bears a legend restricting transfer; minimum 6-month holding period.
Disclosure documents by offering type: registered = prospectus; municipal = official statement; Reg A/private placement/other exempt = offering circular (sometimes 'notice of sale').
rules: Securities Act of 1933 — registration & prospectus delivery for new issues; criminal penalties for fraud.
SEC Rule 501 of Regulation D — accredited investor definition.
SEC Rule 147 — intrastate offering exemption.
SEC Regulation D, Rules 506(b) & 506(c) — private placement exemptions; Form D filing required.
SEC Regulation A, Tier 1 ($20M) and Tier 2 ($75M).
JOBS Act — expanded Regulation A offering ceilings.
SEC Rule 23 (Securities Act) — prohibits representations that SEC has approved any security.
Cooling-off period — minimum 20 calendar days post-filing.
Errata note — Form 144 filings (affiliate resales under Rule 144) must be filed ELECTRONICALLY via EDGAR as of April 13, 2023 (SEC Release 33-11070); paper filings no longer permitted.
MSRB G-32 — disclosure requirements in primary offerings of municipal securities (official statement delivery).
formulas: Underwriter Spread = Public Offering Price (POP) − Price paid to issuer
Reg A Tier 2 non-accredited investment limit = Greater of (10% × net worth) or (10% × annual net income), per offering
Rule 147 in-state nexus test = at least one of: 80% gross revenue in-state, 80% assets in-state, 80% proceeds used in-state, OR majority of employees in-state
mnemonics: 'BRICC' exempt issuers: Banks (not holding cos.), Religious/charitable nonprofits, IRS/U.S. government, Carriers (common), Cities (municipalities). Plus S&Ls.
Reg A tiers — 'Twenty / Seventy-five': Tier 1 = $20M; Tier 2 = $75M.
Accredited income test — '2-3-1': $200K single / $300K joint / $1M net worth (ex-residence).
Red herring activities allowed in cooling-off — 'TIDBI': Tombstones, Indications of interest, Due diligence, Blue-sky, Issue red herrings. (NO sales.)
Private placement stock aliases — 'RULL': Restricted, Unregistered, Letter, Legend.
Firm commitment = Firm (underwriter) risk; Best Efforts = Burden on issuer.

sections.title: Lesson 1.2: Trading Securities in the Secondary Markets
sections.overview: The secondary market — regulated under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (which created the SEC) — is where investors trade previously issued securities among themselves, providing the liquidity that makes the primary market viable. This lesson identifies the four market centers (exchanges, OTC, third market, fourth market/ECNs) and the participants who trade and facilitate those trades (investors, broker-dealers, transfer agents, registrars, clearing agencies, depositories).
key_concepts: In the secondary market, the seller is NEVER the issuer (exception: corporate tender offers/buybacks).
Liquidity = ability to buy/sell easily at a fair price. T-bills and listed stocks are highly liquid; limited partnership units are illiquid.

Four market centers: (1) Exchanges (auction market, listed securities, physical floor — e.g., NYSE); (2) OTC (decentralized electronic interdealer network for unlisted stocks and most bonds, including munis and Treasuries); (3) Third Market / Nasdaq Intermarket (exchange-listed securities traded OTC; trades reported to Consolidated Tape within 10 seconds); (4) Fourth Market (institution-to-institution via ECNs, 24/7, no BDs).

Exchange members: Designated Market Maker (DMM/specialist) — maintains inventory and a fair/orderly market in an assigned security; Floor Broker — represents firm's customer orders; Two-Dollar Broker — assists overwhelmed floor brokers for a fee; Floor Trader (RFT) — trades for firm's own account.
Trading on an exchange occurs only between members, not employees of the exchange.
OTC market makers compete; customer sells at the bid (to dealer) and buys at the ask (from dealer); spread = market maker's profit.
Most corporate bonds, all municipal bonds, and Treasury debt trade OTC.
Dark pools = nonpublic trading venues for large institutional blocks; volume, price, and identity hidden — improves execution for institutions but reduces market transparency.
Trading hours: NYSE 9:30 am – 4:00 pm ET; OTC similar with extended hours (often to 6:30 pm) — wider spreads and higher volatility after hours.
Investors: Retail (own money); Day Traders (rapid intraday, flat at close); Accredited (term mainly used in primary market); Institutional (mutual funds, pensions, banks, insurers, etc.).

Fiduciary = manages assets for a beneficiary; legally must place beneficiary's interest first. Includes custodians (UGMA/UTMA, IRA custodians), trustees, guardians, executors. Investment advisers are ALWAYS fiduciaries.
Investment Adviser three-prong test (ABC): gives Advice, as a regular part of Business, for Compensation — registers under Investment Advisers Act of 1940.

Broker-Dealer types: Carrying/Clearing firm — holds customer funds/securities, executes, clears, settles, sends confirmations; higher net capital required; must segregate customer assets. Fully Disclosed (Introducing) firm — takes orders but uses a clearing firm for custody and back-office; lower net capital. Prime Broker — central account that holds customer assets while customer also uses multiple Executing Brokers.
A BD can be both broker and dealer — but NEVER both on the same transaction.
Transfer agent: issues/cancels certificates, maintains ownership records, handles lost/stolen certificates.
Registrar: separate from issuer and transfer agent; audits the transfer agent; tracks shares authorized vs. outstanding.

Clearing agencies/depositories: DTCC = largest securities depository in the world; provides custody and clears trades. OCC = clearing agent for listed options; standardizes, guarantees, and issues options contracts; sets strike prices and expiration months.
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 — regulates secondary markets; created the SEC; regulates exchanges, OTC, BDs, and SROs.
Investment Advisers Act of 1940 — IA registration; fiduciary standard.
FINRA membership agreement — defines lines of business; firms may never claim SEC/FINRA endorsement or approval.
Carrying firms must segregate customer funds/securities from firm assets (no commingling).
Third-market trades must be reported to the Consolidated Tape within 10 seconds of execution.
Errata note — order-event reporting flows through the Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT) under FINRA Rule 6800 Series; OATS was retired 9/1/2021.
mnemonics: Four markets — 'Exchanges, OTC, Third, Fourth' = 'E-O-T-F' (Exchange listed; OTC unlisted; Third = listed traded OTC; Fourth = institutions via ECN).
IA three-prong test — 'ABC': Advice, Business, Compensation.
BD roles — 'Broker = Agent, Charges Commission; Dealer = Principal, earns Spread.'
DMM duties — 'FOI': Fair & Orderly market, maintain Inventory.

sections.title: Lesson 1.3: Placing a Trade
sections.overview: This lesson covers the mechanics of order entry in the secondary market: how quotes (bid/ask/size/spread) are constructed, the major order types and their time/fill qualifiers, long vs. short positions, principal vs. agency trading capacity, and settlement timelines. Mastery of these mechanics is heavily tested.
key_concepts: Bullish = expects price to rise (long stock, long rights/warrants/calls). Bearish = expects price to fall (short stock, long puts).
Quote = two-sided: Bid (highest price a buyer will pay; where customer SELLS) and Ask/Offer (lowest price a seller will accept; where customer BUYS). Bid is ALWAYS less than ask.
Size = number of round lots (1 round lot = 100 shares) available at each side. Example: 'Bid 42 Ask 42.50 size 10 x 12' means 1,000 shares bid, 1,200 shares offered.
On an exchange the DMM's order book determines the quote: highest open buy limit = bid; lowest open sell limit = ask.
In OTC, the inside quote = highest bid among market makers and lowest ask among market makers (may come from different dealers).
Minimum price increment for stocks ≥$1.00 is $0.01; sub-penny pricing allowed for stocks under $1.00.
Spread = Ask − Bid. Inside market / inside quote = best (highest) bid and best (lowest) ask.
Market order: executed immediately at best available price; always fills (no price guarantee); takes priority over limit orders.
Limit order: buy at limit price or LOWER; sell at limit price or HIGHER. Risk = missing the market (may never execute).

Stop order: not a live order — it's a trigger. When the stock trades AT or THROUGH the stop price, it becomes a market order. Buy stops placed ABOVE current market; sell stops placed BELOW current market.
Stop-limit order: triggered like a stop, but becomes a LIMIT order — execution not guaranteed.
Time qualifiers — Day order (default; expires at close); GTC (good-til-canceled; auto-canceled last business day of April and October if open); Market-at-Open / Market-on-Close.

Fill qualifiers (limit orders only) — FOK (Fill-Or-Kill: fill entire order immediately or cancel; no partial); IOC (Immediate-Or-Cancel: fill what you can immediately, cancel rest; partial OK); AON (All-Or-None: must fill entirely but not immediate; can be day or GTC).
Long position: Buy to open, Sell to close. Max loss = cost basis (security goes to zero). Bullish view.
Short position: Sell to open (borrow & sell), Buy to close (cover). Max loss = UNLIMITED (price can rise indefinitely). Bearish view.
Broker (Agent): trades on customer's behalf; charges a commission; trade is between customer and another party.
Dealer (Principal/Market Maker): trades from own inventory with customer; earns the spread (markup on sales to customers, markdown on purchases from customers).
A BD may act as broker OR dealer on a given trade — never both on the same transaction.

Settlement — Regular way: T+1 for U.S. Treasury securities (bills, notes, bonds) AND for corporate stocks/bonds, municipal debt, agency securities (GNMA), and GSE securities (FNMA, FHLMC). [ERRATA: stocks/munis/corporates moved from T+2 to T+1 effective 5/28/2024 under amended SEC Rule 15c6-1.]
Cash settlement (same-day): securities delivered and payment made on trade date; requires both parties' agreement and immediate availability.
Ex-dividend date under T+1 = same business day as the record date for regular-way trades. [ERRATA: previously one business day before record date under T+2.]
Options settle next business day (T+1) — unchanged.
When-issued trades settle on issuance date — unchanged.
rules: SEC Rule 15c6-1 (as amended) — regular-way settlement is T+1 for most securities (effective May 28, 2024).
Market orders take precedence over limit orders; limit orders execute on a first-come, first-served basis at a given price.
FINRA reporting of secondary-market trades — see CAT (Consolidated Audit Trail) under FINRA Rule 6800 Series for order-event reporting.
A BD must disclose its capacity (agent vs. principal) on the trade confirmation.
formulas: Quote size in shares = Size (in round lots) × 100
Long P/L = Sales Proceeds − Cost Basis
Short P/L = Short Sale Price − Cover (Buy-Back) Price
Settlement Date (regular way, most securities) = Trade Date + 1 business day (T+1)
mnemonics: Bull/Bear — 'Bulls thrust horns UP; Bears swipe claws DOWN.'
Order placement relative to market — 'BLISS / SLOBS': Buy Limits & Sell Stops go BELOW the market; Sell Limits & Buy Stops go ABOVE the market.
Long vs. Short — 'Long = Loss Limited; Short = Sky-high (unlimited) loss.'
Settlement — 'Treasuries, options, and everything else now ride the T+1 train.' (Post-May 2024.)
GTC auto-cancel months — 'April showers, October leaves' (last business day of April and October).
